subject: bio
title: Transport in Mammals
subtitle: Blood, blood vessels, heart structure and cardiac cycle.
concept: The mammalian circulatory system is closed and double (pulmonary + systemic circuits), ensuring oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate.
The heart pumps blood by coordinated contraction; electrical impulses from the SAN control the cardiac cycle.
Haemoglobin loads and unloads O₂ based on partial pressure; the Bohr effect shifts the dissociation curve right in active tissues.

notes.heading: Blood Vessels
items: Arteries: thick muscular/elastic walls; small lumen; carry blood away from heart at high pressure.
Veins: thin walls; large lumen; valves prevent backflow; carry blood to heart at low pressure.
Capillaries: walls one cell thick (squamous endothelium); exchange of materials with tissues by diffusion.
Tissue fluid: formed at arteriole end of capillaries (hydrostatic pressure > osmotic); returned at venule end or via lymph.

notes.heading: Heart Structure and Cardiac Cycle
items: Right side: receives deoxygenated blood; pumps to lungs (pulmonary circuit).
Left side: receives oxygenated blood; pumps to body (systemic circuit). Left ventricle wall is thicker.
Valves: atrioventricular (tricuspid right, bicuspid/mitral left) — prevent backflow to atria; semilunar (pulmonary and aortic) — prevent backflow from arteries.
Cardiac cycle: diastole (relaxation, filling) → atrial systole → ventricular systole → diastole again.
SAN (sinoatrial node) — pacemaker; generates electrical impulse → spreads across atria (contraction) → delayed at AVN → down bundle of His → Purkinje fibres → ventricular contraction.

notes.heading: Haemoglobin and Oxygen Transport
items: Haemoglobin (Hb): 4 polypeptide chains each with a haem group; each haem carries one O₂.
Oxyhaemoglobin: Hb + 4O₂ ⇌ HbO₈ (loaded in lungs; unloaded in tissues).
Oxygen dissociation curve: S-shaped (sigmoidal); cooperativity — binding of first O₂ makes subsequent binding easier.
Bohr effect: increased CO₂ → decreased pH → curve shifts right → Hb has lower affinity for O₂ → more O₂ released in active tissues.
Fetal haemoglobin: higher affinity for O₂ than adult Hb → loads O₂ from maternal haemoglobin across placenta.

definitions.body: A circulatory system with two separate circuits: pulmonary (heart → lungs → heart) and systemic (heart → body → heart).
The decrease in oxygen affinity of haemoglobin caused by an increase in CO₂ concentration (decrease in pH), shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.
The heart's pacemaker — generates rhythmic electrical impulses that spread across the atria to initiate contraction.
Fluid filtered from blood plasma at the arteriole end of capillaries; bathes cells and returns to blood or lymph at the venule end.

workedExamples.q: Explain the Bohr effect and its significance in exercising muscle.

steps.text: Exercising muscles produce CO₂ from aerobic respiration; CO₂ dissolves in blood, forming H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, lowering pH.
H⁺ ions bind to haemoglobin, reducing its affinity for O₂ (allosteric effect) — the oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right.
At the same pO₂, oxyhaemoglobin releases more O₂ to the tissues. This increases O₂ delivery exactly where demand is highest.

mistakes: Confusing atrial and ventricular systole — ventricles contract after atria; ventricles do the powerful pumping.
Describing the tricuspid valve as being on the left side — it is on the RIGHT side (between right atrium and right ventricle).
Forgetting that the Bohr effect INCREASES O₂ delivery to tissues (shifts curve right, not left).
tips: Left ventricle wall is thicker because it pumps blood to the entire systemic circuit at higher pressure.
Fetal Hb curve is to the LEFT of adult Hb — higher affinity (loads from maternal Hb at placenta).
Valve sounds: 'lub' = AV valves closing (ventricular systole); 'dub' = semilunar valves closing (diastole).

flashcards.q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
flashcards.a: The left ventricle pumps blood around the entire systemic circuit at higher pressure; it needs a more muscular wall.
Increased CO₂ reduces Hb's affinity for O₂ (shifts dissociation curve right), increasing O₂ release in active tissues.

flashcards.q: What is the role of the SAN?
flashcards.a: The sinoatrial node is the pacemaker — generates rhythmic electrical impulses that initiate atrial contraction and coordinate the cardiac cycle.
At the arteriole end of capillaries, hydrostatic pressure exceeds osmotic pressure, forcing water and small solutes out of blood plasma into intercellular spaces.

flashcards.q: Why does fetal haemoglobin have a higher affinity for O₂ than adult haemoglobin?
flashcards.a: Fetal Hb binds O₂ from maternal Hb at the placenta; its curve is left-shifted (higher affinity), so it can load O₂ at the pO₂ in the placenta.

flashcards.q: What prevents backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle?
flashcards.a: Semilunar (aortic) valves close when ventricular pressure drops below aortic pressure.

questions.q: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.exp: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.q: The Bohr effect shifts the O₂ dissociation curve to the right. What does this mean?
opts: Hb has higher affinity for O₂
More O₂ is loaded in lungs
More O₂ is released in tissues
questions.exp: Right shift = lower affinity at the same pO₂ = more O₂ unloaded in tissues where CO₂ is high.
The SAN (sinoatrial node) in the right atrium generates the electrical impulse that starts each heartbeat.

questions.q: What is the function of valves in veins?
questions.exp: Venous valves prevent backflow — blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves are essential to ensure one-way flow.

questions.q: At which end of a capillary is tissue fluid absorbed back into the blood?
questions.exp: At the venule end, osmotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure, so tissue fluid is reabsorbed into the capillary.

recall: Describe the differences between arteries, veins and capillaries.
Explain the cardiac cycle and the role of the SAN.
Draw and explain an oxygen dissociation curve.
Explain the Bohr effect and its significance.
Describe how tissue fluid is formed and returned to circulation.
